value.overview: The Spotted Sandpiper (Actitis macularius) is a small, widespread shorebird of the Americas. It breeds mainly across northern North America and migrates south to winter from the southern United States through Central and South America. In Costa Rica it is a regular northern migrant and winter visitor, occurring at both inland wetlands and coastal sites. It usually forages alone along water margins, walking with a characteristic repeated bobbing motion of the rear body and tail.
value.classification: The Spotted Sandpiper belongs to the sandpiper family Scolopacidae in the order Charadriiformes. It is the New World representative of the genus Actitis, which also includes the closely related Common Sandpiper.
value.identification: This compact sandpiper has a brownish back, white underparts, a fairly short straight bill, yellowish to dull yellow legs, and a conspicuous white stripe extending upward between the folded wing and breast. Adults in breeding plumage have bold dark spots across the breast and belly; nonbreeding birds are much plainer below, with spotting greatly reduced or absent. The species is especially recognizable by its persistent tail-bobbing or rump-bobbing while walking. It is about 18–24 cm long.
value.rangeHabitat: The Spotted Sandpiper breeds from Alaska and Canada south through much of the United States, then winters from the southern United States to southern South America. In Costa Rica it is a regular, widespread northern migrant and winter visitor rather than a breeding species. It uses muddy or sandy margins of rivers, streams, ponds, lakes, reservoirs, marshes, estuaries, mangroves, coastal beaches, mudflats, and sandbars. Birds may also occur along rocky streams and quiet edges of disturbed wetlands, from lowlands into the highlands.
value.migrationStatus: Migratory in Costa Rica. Birds occur mainly during southbound migration from approximately August through October and during northbound migration from April through late May; many also remain through the winter period. Costa Rica is not a regular breeding area for the species.
value.breeding: Spotted Sandpipers breed in open or semi-open areas near freshwater, including stream and lake margins, wet meadows, grasslands, forest edges, fields, and sparsely vegetated shorelines. The species has an unusual mating system in which females commonly defend territories and may mate with more than one male, while males perform most incubation and care of the young. Several broods may be produced in a season. There is no reliable evidence that the species regularly breeds in Costa Rica.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of insects and other small invertebrates, including beetles, flies, larvae, worms, crustaceans, mollusks, and spiders. Small fish or other aquatic items may also be taken. In Costa Rica, it forages along exposed wet margins, mudflats, sandbars, and shallow water. It walks steadily while pecking at the surface or probing soft sediment, and may seize prey from floating vegetation or shallow water.
value.behavior: Spotted Sandpipers are usually solitary or widely spaced from other shorebirds, although several may use the same wetland. They walk with a distinctive bobbing motion of the head, body, and tail, sometimes called teetering. When disturbed, they may fly low over the water with rapid wingbeats and show a flashing white wing stripe. Individuals defend feeding space to varying degrees and often remain close to cover or the waterline while foraging.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered broadly stable, although regional monitoring has indicated declines in parts of the breeding range and local changes may occur.
